title: Competitive strategy: Build-versus-buy becomes a portfolio
desc: Balances control, cost, expertise and dependence while scale, agility and overlapping provider roles reshape advantage.

kps.k: The central competitive question is who can turn AI into differentiated legal delivery, not who can purchase the strongest model.
kps.d: The sources locate potential advantage in proprietary knowledge, integrated workflows, client relationships and accountable execution. Ochsner’s Bloomberg Law report describes firms betting that institutional expertise will distinguish otherwise widely available technology. Razorhorse makes a parallel argument for ALSPs, emphasising workflow design, governance and delivery capacity. The AI Imperative records disagreement: proprietary-development proponents expect durable differentiation, while others expect technology and data to become standard and prioritise judgment and relationships. These are competing explanations of defensibility, not established rankings of winners.

qs.q: The firms that have chosen to customize AI have determined their data will make them stand out against peers in a world where every law firm can buy the same tech.
qs.a: Law Firms Capitalize on Internal Data to Stand Out in AI Age · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: The most defensible providers own the operating system, the combination of workflow design, governance, adoption, security, and change management that makes legal work predictable at scale.
qs.a: ALSPs: The Industrialization of Legal Work · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: Build versus buy is usually a portfolio decision, with trade-offs in control, cost, expertise and platform dependence.
kps.d: Kitishian’s firm profiles contrast Kirkland’s proposed capital-efficient buying strategy, Baker McKenzie’s proprietary service creation and Linklaters’ build–borrow–buy approach. Actual sourcing often combines these categories: firms build applications on external foundation models, co-develop products and retain commercial tools. Freshfields explicitly maintains multiple providers; Polsinelli customises commercial products without seeking to compete with technology companies. Earlier business-model research also distinguishes buying software from outsourcing legal workflows and argues that equity stakes or joint ventures may reduce dependence. No supplied comparison establishes a universally superior sourcing strategy.

qs.q: This strategy is explicitly built on a “buy, borrow, or build” philosophy, a portfolio management approach that balances internal development with external partnerships to optimize for control, capability, and cost.
qs.a: Linklaters AI: Strategic Positioning in Legal AI · Market & press · 2025

qs.q: This is a sensible approach for gaining immediate capabilities, but it again underscores the distinctiveness of Baker McKenzie’s dual strategy of both adopting best-in-class external tools and simultaneously building its own proprietary platforms.
qs.a: Baker McKenzie AI: Strategic Positioning in Legal AI · Market & press · 2025

kps.k: Kirkland’s reported investment illustrates why strategic classifications must remain time-bound.
kps.d: Kitishian’s July 2025 analysis inferred a buying-oriented strategy from public information and found no evidence of substantial developer recruitment; it did not establish that internal capabilities were absent. The Financial Times subsequently reported in May 2026 a $500 million allocation for custom AI, including more than $100 million expected that year, financed from revenue at an initial cost to partner distributions. Bloomberg Law also reported recruitment and a launched private-equity fundraising platform. These developments qualify the earlier characterisation, but neither planned spending nor a product launch demonstrates commercial returns, whole-mandate capability or development of an in-house foundation model.

qs.q: While competitors like DLA Piper are making significant investments in building proprietary, in-house AI tools, K&E’s approach appears to be fundamentally different.58 An examination of the firm’s public statements and hiring patterns reveals no evidence of a large, internal “AI lab” or a significant recruitment drive for AI developers.
qs.a: Kirkland & Ellis AI: Strategic Positioning in Legal AI · Market & press · 2025

qs.q: On Thursday, the firm launched a platform for private equity fundraising it said is “built around Kirkland’s institutional knowledge, workflows and legal judgment.”  How far Kirkland will push into the technical side of building AI is unclear.
qs.a: Law Firms Capitalize on Internal Data to Stand Out in AI Age · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: Scale may reinforce incumbent advantages, but agility and clearer incentives could favour smaller firms and in-house teams.
kps.d: Schenker’s 2026 Bloomberg Law report argues that large firms can absorb development or subscription costs and influence vendors’ roadmaps. Its 2025 spending evidence covers technology generally, not AI alone: 66 firms reported both expenditure categories and classified their own spending, limiting comparisons. Ford’s GC offers a counterargument: smaller firms may adapt faster and depend less on associate-pyramid economics, while in-house departments possess company-specific knowledge and capture time savings directly. McNairn cites a Law360 survey showing more frequent generative-AI use in-house despite higher law-firm spending. The disagreement concerns whether capital and scale outweigh organisational friction, not whether either guarantees success.

qs.q: Big Law firms “have the scale to really absorb the cost of AI, whether that’s through build or buy,” Rusanow added.
qs.a: Law Firm Tech Budgets Drive the Build Versus Buy AI Debate · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: Smaller firms are also less beholden to the pyramid economics that underpin Big Law's profit model—and Big Law's historical advantages associated with economies of scale and the ability to provide "one stop" legal services may become somewhat smaller in an AI world.
qs.a: Ford Motor GC to Law Firms: We Are Outpacing Your AI Adoption · In-house counsel · 2026

kps.k: AI blurs market boundaries as firms, ALSPs, platforms and corporate departments build overlapping capabilities.
kps.d: The Scrambled Competitive Map distinguishes vendors selling tools from AI-native firms delivering legal work, while showing that both can depend on the same foundation-model platforms. Historical Big Four acquisitions and alliances demonstrate that integrated legal, technical and business services predate generative AI; they do not establish subsequent market dominance. More recent sources describe platform entry and capital-backed deployment businesses as additional competitive pressures. Countervailing evidence includes leading firms’ continuing profitability and the Big Four’s limited penetration of established high-end markets. Predictions of consolidation and displacement therefore remain distinct from reported investments, acquisitions and entry.

qs.q: It is that the lines between them are dissolving, and the same actor will sit on several sides at once.
qs.a: The Scrambled Competitive Map · Academia · 2026

qs.q: EY Law’s acquisitions of  Riverview Law in September 2018 (Cohen, 2018) and of Thomson Reuters’ Pangea3 Legal  Managed Service in April 2019 (Tuahene, 2019) signal the Big Four’s intention to combine  the AI-enabled business models we have identified.
qs.a: AI-enabled business models in legal services: from traditional law firms to next-generation law companies? · Academia · 2020

kps.k: Reported deployments support practical capability building, but provide limited evidence of durable competitive superiority.
kps.d: Examples include BakerML’s cross-border employment tool, Linklaters’ substantial Laila usage, A&O Shearman’s multidisciplinary development and The AI Imperative’s financial-services case reporting 5–8% productivity benefits. Their evidential meanings differ: usage measures adoption, awards recognise initiatives, and Baker McKenzie’s reported 100% substantive accuracy came from its own lawyers’ testing. Interview-based research also reports abandoned pilots. Kitishian’s forecasts of dominance for several firms rely on strategic inference and uneven public disclosure, not a common comparative performance test or demonstrated market-share gains.

qs.q: Rigorous testing conducted by Baker McKenzie’s own lawyers demonstrated 100% substantive legal accuracy.
qs.a: Baker McKenzie AI: Strategic Positioning in Legal AI · Market & press · 2025

qs.q: The impact included 5–8% productivity across drafting and review capabilities alongside the foundations for long term                                                                            sustainable adoption.
qs.a: The AI Imperative: Reshaping of the Legal Industry · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: The economic dispute concerns whether AI expands existing practices or replaces associate-heavy delivery models.
kps.d: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Law Firms’ Business Models finds no replacement plans among its interviewees and expects AI to help meet growing demand. AI-native analyses instead point to Covenant’s reported $900 agreement reviews, roughly 90% below traditional pricing, as evidence of alternative delivery economics. Claims that technology costs scale logarithmically, or that small teams can match much larger firms, remain premises or projections rather than market-wide findings. Productised services and subscription or value-based fees could let providers capture efficiency gains, but automation can also cannibalise hourly revenue. Elite-boutique scenarios preserve premium judgment while acknowledging that this positioning cannot accommodate every firm.

qs.q: There was no indication of this in the operational plans of these firms, and it will likely turn out that AI technologies will become useful tools that allow law firms to keep up with client demand and increasing complexity.
qs.a: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Law Firms' Business Models · Academia · 2025

qs.q: The firm operates with only six lawyers handling highly leveraged work, offering limited partnership agreement reviews at $900 per document – approximately 90 per cent less than traditional pricing – while achieving 80-90 per cent reductions in time and cost.[[9]](#_edn9)  This economic model creates profound implications.
qs.a: The AI-native law firm: regulatory innovation and the fundamental restructuring of legal service delivery · Market & press · 2025

kps.k: Corporate buyers may drive change through both insourcing and demands for demonstrable improvements from providers.
kps.d: Ford’s GC reports faster internal adoption than observed among outside counsel and promises to reward net savings, while explicitly limiting these observations to one company’s early experience. Salesforce asks firms and ALSPs to share gains through better service, lower costs and expanded pro bono capacity rather than retain them solely as margin. Other buyer examples describe co-designed workflows and quality benchmarking. Yet Freshfields’ Perez warns that client acceptance can constrain deployment even when technology and staff are ready. Client demand therefore ranges from active redesign to caution; reported understaffing and potential insourcing do not prove that outsourced work has already migrated.

qs.q: But from the vantage point of one large public company, here are some early takeaways.
qs.a: Ford Motor GC to Law Firms: We Are Outpacing Your AI Adoption · In-house counsel · 2026

qs.q: When AI reduces time and cost, and when AI expands the capacity of your teams, those savings must be passed along to clients and invested into communities via pro bono efforts, not just used to improve firm margins.
qs.a: How Law Firms Can Lead the Agentic AI Era — And What Clients Now Expect · In-house counsel · 2026

kps.k: Practical strategy requires governed workflows, sustained organisational investment and measurement beyond adoption.
kps.d: The sources recommend multidisciplinary teams, protected funding, client collaboration and scaling successful pilots rather than indiscriminate spending. Governance must cover confidentiality, privilege, human verification and clear escalation responsibilities. Linklaters’ reported LinksAI results retain an expert-supervision requirement despite model improvements; proprietary ownership does not itself establish reliability. The AI Imperative adds investment tracking and control of token and API costs. A 2026 market analysis cites an association between clear AI strategy and tangible returns, not causation. The practical implication is to assess quality, net client value and sustainable matter economics separately from spending, tool availability and usage.

qs.q: •    Ring-fence funding to insulate innovation from short-term pressures.
qs.a: Law in the Era of AI: Clients, Firms, and the Future of the Legal Industry · Academia · 2026

qs.q: AI enhances this system, but it does not replace the need for accountability, escalation paths, and human ownership when things go wrong.
qs.a: ALSPs: The Industrialization of Legal Work · Market & press · 2026

vlens.an: The supplied legal-tech-vendor voice does not reject the cluster’s account of build-versus-buy portfolios, differentiated delivery or overlapping provider roles, but shifts the principal competitive lens from law firms’ sourcing strategies to actual AI adoption within corporate legal departments. McNairn argues that in-house teams may lead despite lower spending because they capture time savings directly, serve a single corporate client and face executive pressure to demonstrate AI use; by contrast, law-firm efficiencies create tensions around realisation, staffing, pricing and the billable hour. He still treats law-firm-first vendors such as Harvey, Spellbook and Lora as contenders for the in-house market, without identifying a winner. Because the evidence contains only one curated vendor source, it does not support claims about shared views or internal variation across legal-tech vendors; the material variation is within McNairn’s argument, which acknowledges greater law-firm expenditure while prioritising frequency of use and buyer-side incentives as more meaningful indicators.

qs.q: According to a law 360 survey released earlier this year, more than half of in-house lawyers now use generative AI at least three times a week compared with fewer than half of law firm lawyers.
qs.a: Ross McNairn — Wordsmith.ai (in-house legal orchestration) · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: Every hour that AI saves an in-house lawyer is an obvious win.
qs.a: Ross McNairn — Wordsmith.ai (in-house legal orchestration) · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

vlens.an: The selected academia and research sources collectively accept the proposition that competitive advantage lies in differentiated, integrated legal delivery rather than access to a model alone, and materially develop its portfolio logic. Common explanations include the need to combine internal development, acquisitions, alliances, multiple vendors, multidisciplinary expertise and integration with client systems; to manage platform dependence through equity, joint ventures or shared control; and to support implementation through governance, protected funding, experimentation and organisational reform. Material variation concerns where change will originate and who benefits: some sources emphasise incumbent law firms’ capacity for incremental innovation and financially stronger firms’ scale advantages; others foreground the Big Four’s integrated capabilities, AI-native or foundation-model deployment providers, or corporate legal departments as catalysts for insourcing and ecosystem change. One research framework presents advisory specialisation, external contracting and vertical integration as alternative strategic responses rather than prescribing one universal portfolio. The sources also differ on economic effects: interview-based research chiefly anticipates augmentation and demand growth, whereas other analyses predict greater pressure on associate-heavy delivery models. Across these accounts, acquisitions, pilots, investments and alliances evidence capability-building or strategic intent, while durable superiority, widespread work migration and future displacement remain unproven or predictive. This assessment concerns only the curated sources supplied, not academia and research generally.

qs.q: •    Adopt a “buy-and-build” strategy, partnering for scale and expertise the law             ﬁrm doesn’t have.
qs.a: Law in the Era of AI: Clients, Firms, and the Future of the Legal Industry · Academia · 2026

qs.q: This has led many firms to diversify by establishing tentative relationships with multiple  providers.
qs.a: AI-enabled business models in legal services: from traditional law firms to next-generation law companies? · Academia · 2020

vlens.an: The selected in-house counsel and legal-operations sources accept the proposition that competitive advantage depends on converting AI into differentiated, integrated and accountable legal delivery rather than merely acquiring a strong model. They materially extend it with a buyer-side test of value: providers must translate AI-enabled capacity into better service, measurable net savings and efficiency gains shared with clients. Common reasons include the importance of company-specific knowledge, workflow integration, organisational adaptability, governance and human verification. There is material variation within this professional voice. Ford’s GC emphasises the potential structural advantage of tailored in-house tools and smaller-firm agility, based explicitly on one company’s preliminary experience, while leaving competitive outcomes uncertain. Salesforce is more prescriptive about integrated commercial solutions, unified client intelligence, governance and shared gains across firms and ALSPs, but its market-share claims are forecasts unsupported by quantified performance evidence. These curated sources therefore develop the proposition without establishing that their expectations are representative of in-house counsel or legal operations generally.

qs.q: AI legal solutions developed internally may therefore serve company needs with greater continuous fidelity and efficacy, which could be a major structural advantage for in-house legal departments over external legal-service providers.
qs.a: Ford Motor GC to Law Firms: We Are Outpacing Your AI Adoption · In-house counsel · 2026

qs.q: Heightened effectiveness and efficiency gains from AI, **shared with clients**, are no longer optional nice-to-haves; they’re prerequisites for staying competitive and seizing revenue opportunities.
qs.a: How Law Firms Can Lead the Agentic AI Era — And What Clients Now Expect · In-house counsel · 2026

vlens.an: This curated set of market-analyst, consultancy and press sources broadly accepts the proposition that build-versus-buy has become a portfolio decision and that advantage depends more on differentiated delivery than on access to a strong underlying model. Common reasons include the value of proprietary knowledge and client data; the need to combine commercial tools, internal applications and partnerships; and the importance of workflow integration, governance, adoption, multidisciplinary talent, client confidence and cost control. Collectively, the sources materially extend the proposition by describing buyer co-design and benchmarking of workflows, AI-native and platform-based delivery models, changing staffing and pricing structures, and competitive pressure from ALSPs, open-source projects and foundation-model providers. Material variation concerns confidence and emphasis rather than rejection of the core: consultancy-style firm profiles often predict leadership or dominance from integrated strategies; press reports are generally more cautious, distinguishing investment and product launches from proven returns; scale-focused analysis stresses that proprietary development may be unaffordable outside the largest firms; and AI-native commentary predicts structural displacement more strongly than the cluster synthesis supports. Other sources preserve a larger role for commercial vendors, human judgment and client relationships. Across these differences, reported deployments show adoption and some productivity or operational gains, but not durable comparative superiority. The sources are a curated selection and should not be treated as representative of all analysts, consultancies or press coverage.

qs.q: In part, this is due to AI                                                                                no clear consensus or single best-practice strategy, and most firms are pursuing some investments sitting across a range of areas and increasingly                                                                                combination of building, buying, and partnering.
qs.a: The AI Imperative: Reshaping of the Legal Industry · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: One large technology company's legal department co-designs AI workflows with outside counsel, mandating specific tool use at specific workflow stages and benchmarking quality outcomes against best-attorney baselines.
qs.a: The 4 Scenarios: Which Law Firm Business Model Are You Building? · Market & press · 2026

vlens.an: This professional-body source accepts the proposition that competitive advantage comes from differentiated legal delivery rather than access to AI alone. It locates that differentiation particularly in proprietary tools customised to firm-specific workflows, linking them to efficiency, service quality and stronger market positioning. It materially extends the proposition by suggesting that firms developing these capabilities could become providers of lawyer-designed technology and services in adjacent markets. Its framing is more build-centric than the cluster’s portfolio approach and places greater weight on large firms’ financial capacity. There is also internal qualification: the source acknowledges that AI may strengthen smaller firms and benefit access to justice, while urging continued foundational legal and practical training. These caveats do not reverse its overall support, although its claims that the new market is exclusive to developing firms and presently lacks providers are asserted more strongly than the supplied evidence supports.

qs.q: The ability to build proprietary AI solutions provides large firms with a unique edge, enabling them to tailor AI tools to their specific needs and workflows.
qs.a: The Future is Now: Artificial Intelligence and the Legal Profession · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: Additionally, the data shows that this opportunity opens up for these firms, and only these firms, the possibility to participate in a new market by offering services and technology designed by lawyers and for lawyers, which does not preclude them from adapting to other industries and uses.
qs.a: The Future is Now: Artificial Intelligence and the Legal Profession · Regulators & courts · 2024

vlens.an: The traditional law-firm voice represented here supports the proposition that competitive advantage depends less on acquiring a leading model than on combining legal expertise with practical deployment, integrated workflows and multidisciplinary execution. A&O Shearman presents advisory capability and solution-building as mutually reinforcing: lawyers, developers and technologists build tools for internal and client use, while lawyer adoption, training and practical experience inform product refinement. This also fits the proposition’s portfolio logic because the emphasis is on tailoring and integrating AI rather than developing a foundation model. Materially, however, the account is a firm-authored description of its own strategy. Its evidence establishes reported deployment practices and claimed differentiation, not comparative performance, commercial returns or durable competitive superiority. Because this facet contains one curated firm source, it should not be treated as representative of traditional law firms generally.

qs.q: The breadth and depth of our expertise, combined with the insights generated from building and deploying systems, puts us at the forefront of the marketplace with our AI adoption and advisory capabilities.
qs.a: AI leadership: Practicing what we preach · Law firms · 2025

qs.q: Through our Markets Innovation Group (MIG), a practice comprising lawyers, developers, and technologists, we continue to innovate by building generative AI solutions used internally and directly by our clients.
qs.a: AI leadership: Practicing what we preach · Law firms · 2025

elens.an: The 2015–2022 material accepts the proposition’s core portfolio logic and gives it an earlier, organisational foundation. It shows that competitive capability was already being assembled through combinations of acquisitions, technology alliances, outsourced legal workflows, relationships with multiple vendors, equity stakes, joint ventures and internal legal-operations capabilities—not through a simple choice between building or purchasing one technology. The Big Four-focused records emphasise integrated legal, technical and business-service capacity, using Deloitte’s acquisitions and alliance with Kira Systems as evidence of strategic intent. The law-firm business-model source extends this into a concrete three-part framework: specialise in human legal advice, contract with external providers, or vertically integrate new capabilities. It also identifies control and dependence as governance questions, proposing shared ownership and joint ventures as intermediate options. Material variation lies mainly in the actor and organisational route: the Big Four examples concern entrants assembling broad integrated offerings, whereas the law-firm analysis compares external diversification with internal integration and advisory specialisation. The evidence remains qualified: these sources document strategies, transactions and inferred intentions rather than durable competitive superiority or measured client outcomes, and they note constraints from implementation scale, partnership governance and regulation. Two records appear to cover versions of the same Big Four source, so they should not be treated as independent evidence of prevalence; in any event, this curated set does not represent all sources from the period.

elens.an: The 2023–2024 source accepts the proposition’s core claim that competitive advantage depends on converting AI into differentiated legal delivery rather than merely acquiring technology. It locates that differentiation in proprietary, workflow-specific tools that may improve efficiency, service quality and market position. It materially extends the proposition by proposing that firms with internal development capabilities could enter adjacent markets for lawyer-designed technology and services. Internal variation qualifies its large-firm emphasis: greater financial capacity is offered only as a probable explanation for larger firms’ lead; AI may also strengthen smaller firms; and foundational lawyer training remains necessary. Its stronger claims—that proprietary development is a significant advantage, that the opportunity belongs only to developing firms, and that client demand is currently unmet—go beyond the evidence described and do not establish durable competitive superiority.

elens.an: The curated 2025 sources accept the synthesis’s principal proposition that competitive advantage depends on differentiated, integrated legal delivery rather than access to a strong model alone, and materially develop it with concrete strategies for adoption at scale. Their common reasoning is that firms must combine sourcing choices with proprietary knowledge, workflow integration, multidisciplinary teams, training, governance, client relationships and sustained investment. Linklaters, Baker McKenzie, DLA Piper, A&O Shearman and Freshfields illustrate different portfolio configurations: internal applications built on external models, commercial tools, co-development, multiple vendors and, in Baker McKenzie’s case, equity-backed ventures. Kirkland is framed instead as an ecosystem-based buyer whose advantage would come from capital, transactional data and effective deployment. Material variation concerns the economic end state. The law-firm accounts and interview research generally envisage augmentation, capacity expansion and stronger incumbent differentiation, while the AI-native analysis argues that technology can become the principal leverage mechanism and displace associate-heavy delivery. The sources also vary in evidential strength: reported usage, pilots and deployed tools establish practical capability building, but claims of durable dominance, logarithmic technology scaling or inevitable displacement remain predictions rather than demonstrated comparative outcomes. Client acceptance, failed pilots, billable-hour incentives, verification, confidentiality and coordination are recurring constraints, so adoption at scale is presented as an organisational and commercial achievement rather than simple tool rollout.

qs.q: This strategy is explicitly built on a “buy, borrow, or build” philosophy, a portfolio management approach that balances internal development with external partnerships to optimize for control, capability, and cost.
qs.a: Linklaters AI: Strategic Positioning in Legal AI · Market & press · 2025

qs.q: Covenant, co-founded by Jen Berrent (former CLO/COO of WeWork) and Richard Perris (formerly of CVC Capital Partners and Clifford Chance), received $4m in seed funding with an explicit premise: that technology is the main leverage.
qs.a: The AI-native law firm: regulatory innovation and the fundamental restructuring of legal service delivery · Market & press · 2025

elens.an:
The curated 2026 sources collectively accept the proposition that build-versus-buy has become a portfolio decision and materially develop it into a broader account of competitive delivery. Common reasoning is that access to a strong model is insufficient: advantage is instead associated with proprietary organisational knowledge, workflow integration, governance, multidisciplinary capability, client-system integration, human accountability and measurable client value. The period adds concrete evidence of hybrid sourcing, including custom applications built on external models, commercial tools supplemented by proprietary capabilities, partnerships and major internal investment. It also expands the competitive map beyond law firms and legal-tech vendors to include AI-native legal providers, ALSPs, foundation-model platforms, deployment businesses and corporate legal departments.

Material variation concerns where advantage will accrue. Some sources emphasise the capital, data and purchasing influence of large firms, exemplified by Kirkland’s planned $500 million proprietary platform; others argue that smaller firms’ agility or in-house teams’ company-specific knowledge and clearer incentives may outweigh scale. Buyer-side sources further develop the proposition by making co-designed workflows, shared efficiency gains and net savings conditions of provider selection. McNairn redirects attention most clearly from provider sourcing strategy to actual in-house adoption, but this changes the centre of analysis rather than rejecting the portfolio proposition. Sources also differ on future delivery economics: some envisage platform-based or AI-native substitution for associate-heavy work, while others preserve premium human-led practice augmented by AI. Across these positions, reported investments, adoption and isolated productivity or recovery figures do not establish durable superiority; consolidation, displacement and market-share claims remain forecasts. Because these are selected sources rather than a survey, their alignment should not be read as evidence of prevalence across any stakeholder group.

qs.q: In part, this is due to AI                                                                                no clear consensus or single best-practice strategy, and most firms are pursuing some investments sitting across a range of areas and increasingly                                                                                combination of building, buying, and partnering.
